Architecture

≈1.5k · checked 2026-09-02 · How this system is put together and where things belong — the three planes, the pipeline, and the boundaries that must not be crossed

What this project is

Aya's Playground is a marketplace for buying and selling CTF challenges. Authors list a challenge; buyers purchase it and receive a ready-to-deploy bundle for their own event or practice. v1 sells Cryptography challenges only — the taxonomy is data, so other categories are configuration rather than code, but nothing else is enabled yet.

It is deliberately not a CTF hosting platform. It does not run events, does not host live challenge instances, and does not keep a scoreboard. It sells the artifact; the buyer runs it on their own CTFd (or anything else). See decisions/0002-three-plane-architecture.

Shape of the system — three planes

PlaneResponsibilityTalks to
CatalogChallenges, immutable versions, listings, crypto-scheme taxonomy, search, purchase-gated reviewsStore, Forge (for verification state)
ForgeThe sandbox. Builds a challenge for a given flag, verifies it is solvable, fulfills an orderDocker, Queue, Store
CommerceOrders, Midtrans payments, escrow, licenses, signed delivery, payout balancesMidtrans, Forge (fulfillment), Store

The pipeline runs left to right, and every stage is persisted:

submit → build → verify → publish → order → fulfill → deliver
         └──────┬──────┘                     └──┬──┘
             Forge sandbox                 same Forge sandbox

build, verify, and fulfill are three callers of one sandbox primitive. Fulfillment re-runs the seller's generator with the buyer's flag, which is why the sandbox sits on the order critical path and why fulfillment is a queued job with retry rather than a synchronous request. See decisions/0003-flag-modes.

Where code goes

src/app/           Next.js App Router — pages and route handlers.
                   Route handlers validate input, call a plane, and shape a response.
                   They hold NO business logic.
src/components/    React components, PascalCase files.
src/lib/core/      Shared contracts: bundle schema, flag derivation, license types,
                   error taxonomy, id generation. Imported by every plane; imports none.
src/lib/catalog/   Challenges, versions, listings, taxonomy, reviews, search.
src/lib/forge/     Runner contract, docker runner, stub runner, build/verify/fulfill, queue.
src/lib/commerce/  Orders, order state machine, Midtrans client + webhook, escrow,
                   licenses, delivery tokens, payout balances.
src/lib/auth/      Sessions, users, route guards.
src/lib/store/     Persistence behind one interface: memory (default) + Postgres.
src/lib/audit/     Append-only audit log.
deploy/runner/     Sandbox images — python-crypto, sage.
test/              Integration and contract tests; unit tests sit beside their source.

Dependency direction is one-way: core ← planes ← app. A plane never imports another plane's internals — only its public entry module and core.

Boundaries that matter

  1. Seller-supplied code executes only inside the Forge sandbox. No code path in the Next.js process ever evaluates, imports, or spawns bundle content. This is the rule whose violation is remote code execution on the host. See security-guardrails.
  2. A listing publishes only against a passing verification bound to its exact version hash. Change the bundle, and the hash changes, the verification is invalidated, and the listing auto-unpublishes. A "Verified" badge that can drift from what it verified is worse than no badge.
  3. Flags are derived, never stored in plaintext. flag = KDF(server_secret, order). There is no flag column to leak.
  4. Order state changes only through the state machine, driven by signature-verified Midtrans webhooks. A client redirect never moves money. See commerce.
  5. The UI never reaches the store directly. It goes through a plane, which is where authorization lives.

What is intentionally simple

  • The store defaults to in-memory. npm run dev boots with no Postgres and no Docker. This is what keeps the project runnable, and it is not a bug to fix. Set DATABASE_URL and the identical interface is served by Postgres instead — test/store-contract.test.ts runs one suite against both, so what the tests prove about development is also true of production.

Two things only the database can give, and they are why it exists: compareAndSet becomes UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND state = $2, atomic across processes, so a duplicated webhook handled by two workers cannot double-transition an order; and the download counter and payout arithmetic become single statements rather than read-modify-write.

  • Payouts are a recorded balance an admin releases by hand. Automated disbursement means KYC onboarding, and v1 does not have the volume to justify it.
  • Search is a SQL/array filter, not a search engine. A crypto-only catalog is small. Adding Elasticsearch before there is anything to search is the wrong trade.

Process-wide state

The store, the sandbox runner, and the job queue are globalThis-backed singletons (src/lib/core/singleton.ts), not module-level lets.

This is not a style preference. Next.js compiles route handlers into separate module registries, so with a plain module-level variable, /api/auth/register and /api/auth/login each get their own in-memory store — registering a user and then failing to find them. That bug is silent, and it looks like a password problem.

One consequence to know in development: a globalThis instance survives hot reload, so a code change to the runner or the store does not take effect until the dev server restarts.

See also: conventions, security-guardrails, domain-model, glossary.

Context discipline

≈444 · never verified · Deciding what to read before reading it — applies to every task in this repository

Loading everything is not thoroughness. It is the most common way an agent runs out of room to think, and it degrades quietly: nothing fails, answers just get worse as the useful context is crowded out by material nobody needed.

Read the index first

wondev build writes a memory index listing every document with its approximate token cost and the condition under which it is worth reading. Read that, then load only what matches. Documents marked always: true are already in your context — you do not need to open them.

Read a section, not a file

For a large document, find the heading you need with a search and read that section. Opening a 15k-token file to use 300 tokens of it is the same mistake as loading the whole set.

Prefer structure over text search

If a tool that indexes this codebase's symbols is available, ask it who calls what and where a symbol is defined before falling back to grep plus reading files. A structural answer arrives with file and line attached and costs a fraction of the reading.

Do not infer cross-service behaviour from a code index. Message channels, environment contracts, and proxy configuration are invisible to it — those live in the memory documents.

Hand off wide investigations

When a question spans more of the codebase than fits comfortably, dispatch a subagent and ask it to return conclusions rather than file contents. The point of delegation is that its reading happens in its context, not yours.

Keep this true

A stale document is worse than a missing one, because it is trusted. When a document is reconciled against the code, stamp it:

verified: 2026-08-11
verifiedAgainst: what you actually checked it against

wondev check reports documents that have never been verified.

Conventions

≈1.2k · checked 2026-09-02 · How code in this repository is written, named, tested, and reviewed

Language and tooling

TypeScript, a single Next.js 14 App Router app on npm, code under src/. Frontend is Tailwind + shadcn/ui. Persistence is Postgres via pg, behind a store interface whose default implementation is in-memory.

install:      npm install
dev:          npm run dev
build:        npm run build          # next build
test:         npm test               # vitest run
lint:         npm run lint           # next lint
typecheck:    npm run typecheck      # tsc --noEmit
verify:       npm run verify         # typecheck + lint + test + build
runner:build: npm run runner:build   # sandbox images (needs Docker)
seed:         npm run seed           # example challenges into a running server
db:migrate:   npm run db:migrate     # apply schema.sql to DATABASE_URL

The Postgres half of the store contract suite is skipped unless DATABASE_URL is set. Run it before touching postgres.ts, against a separate database — the suite truncates every table before each test:

docker compose up -d
docker compose exec db createdb -U aya aya_test
DATABASE_URL=postgres://aya:aya@localhost:5433/aya_test npm run db:migrate
DATABASE_URL=postgres://aya:aya@localhost:5433/aya_test npm test -- store-contract

PostgresStore.reset() refuses a database whose name does not contain "test". That guard is the only thing between the test suite and development data, so do not name a working database ..._test.

Naming

  • Files: kebab-case — order-state-machine.ts, docker-runner.ts.
  • React components: PascalCase files under src/components/ — ListingCard.tsx.
  • Types and interfaces: PascalCase, no I prefix — SandboxRunner, not ISandboxRunner.
  • Tests sit beside their source as <name>.test.ts; cross-plane tests live in test/.

Testing

vitest. TDD where practical: write the failing test first for anything in core/ or any state transition.

Two things require exhaustive tests, not representative ones:

  1. The order state machine — every transition in the table, and every transition not in the table asserted to be rejected. Money moves here.
  2. The sandbox argument builder — assert every isolation flag is present in the generated docker run argv. That test is a security control that happens to be written in vitest; treat a change to it with the seriousness of changing a firewall rule.

Everything in src/lib/core/ has tests. Anything parsing untrusted input — challenge.yml, webhook bodies, uploaded archives — needs a malformed-input case, not only a happy path.

A change to either store implementation goes in test/store-contract.test.ts, which runs one suite against both. A test written against only the in-memory store proves nothing about what production does.

Error handling

Expected, handled conditions — a rejected bundle, a failed verification, a declined payment, an expired download token — return a structured error from the taxonomy in src/lib/core/ and are written to the audit log. Programming bugs crash loudly; do not wrap a plane in a catch-all that turns a bug into a 200.

Never return a raw sandbox stderr to a buyer. It is seller code output and may contain the flag or the solution.

Comments

Comment the why, never restate the what. The highest-value comments in this codebase explain a security decision — why an isolation flag is set, why a check happens before rather than after a normalization step.

What not to do

  • Never execute bundle content outside the Forge sandbox — no require, no eval, no child_process on seller files. See security-guardrails.
  • Never let the stub runner emit a passed verdict. It exists so the app boots without Docker; if it can pass a verification, the badge is a lie.
  • Never trust a Midtrans client redirect to move an order forward. Webhook only, signature verified. See commerce.
  • Never store a flag in plaintext, and never log one — not in the audit log, not in an error, not in a sandbox output capture that gets persisted.
  • Never put business logic in a route handler. If a handler is longer than input validation plus one plane call plus a response, the logic belongs in a plane.
  • Never commit secrets. AYA_FLAG_SECRET, MIDTRANS_SERVER_KEY, and AYA_AUTH_SECRET come from env and fail closed when unset in production.
  • Never import src/lib/core/flag.ts from a client component. It reaches for node:crypto and would put flag derivation in the browser bundle. Pure format helpers live in flag-format.ts, which a client component may import; the split is a boundary, not a convenience.
  • Never hold process-wide state in a module-level let. Use src/lib/core/singleton.ts — see the note in architecture for the bug this prevents.

See also: architecture, security-guardrails.

Security guardrails

≈1.4k · never verified · Non-negotiable rules for executing seller code and handling money — sandbox isolation, flag secrecy, payment integrity

This marketplace runs arbitrary code written by strangers and moves real money. These are hard requirements, not configuration.

The sandbox

Every execution of seller-supplied code — build, verify, or fulfill — runs in a container with all of the following. There is no "just this once" path.

ControlSettingWhy
Network--network=noneA crypto challenge never needs network. This removes exfiltration and pivoting outright.
Root filesystem--read-onlyNothing persists outside the declared output mount.
Writable space--tmpfs /tmp with a size capBounded scratch; a fork-bomb of files cannot fill the host disk.
User--user 65534:65534Never root, even inside the container.
Capabilities--cap-drop=ALLNo CAP_NET_RAW, no CAP_SYS_PTRACE.
Privilege escalation--security-opt=no-new-privilegesDefeats setuid tricks.
Memory--memory capAn OOM inside the container is a failed run, not a dead host.
CPU--cpus=1One tenant cannot starve the queue.
Processes--pids-limitFork-bomb containment.
Wall clockhost-side timeout, then docker killA while True is a failed run. Do not rely on the container to stop itself.
Outputcaptured, byte-capped, truncatedUnbounded stdout is a memory exhaustion vector on the host.

Input is mounted read-only; exactly one writable output directory is mounted. No host path outside the run directory is ever mounted, and the run directory is created per-run under a dedicated root and deleted afterwards.

Archive extraction is a security boundary of its own. An uploaded bundle is a zip/tar from a stranger. Reject path traversal (../), absolute paths, symlinks pointing outside the tree, and enforce a total-uncompressed-size and file-count cap before writing a single byte — a zip bomb must be refused during inspection, not discovered during extraction.

The stub runner

stubRunner exists so npm run dev works without Docker. It validates structure and returns a verdict of unverified. It can never return passed. If a code path lets it, the "Verified solvable" badge — the entire trust proposition of this marketplace — becomes a claim nobody checked.

Flags

  • Derived, never stored: flag = KDF(AYA_FLAG_SECRET, challengeVersionId + orderId).
  • AYA_FLAG_SECRET is required in production and fails closed when unset.
  • Never logged. Not in the audit trail, not in an error, not in a persisted sandbox capture. Sandbox output is scrubbed for the run's flag before it is stored or shown.
  • Verification uses an ephemeral random flag, never a buyer's derived flag.
  • Seller-facing and admin-facing views never show a buyer's flag.

Money

  • Order state advances only on a Midtrans webhook whose signature verifies as sha512(order_id + status_code + gross_amount + MIDTRANS_SERVER_KEY). A client returning from the payment page proves nothing.
  • Webhooks retry, arrive out of order, and duplicate. Every transition is idempotent, and a transition that is not legal from the current state is refused and audited rather than applied.
  • The authoritative amount is the one the server computed at order creation, never a value read back from the request body.
  • Funds are held through the dispute window before a seller balance becomes payable.

Audit log

Append-only. Who / what / when for every: bundle submission, sandbox run, verification verdict, publish/unpublish, order transition, delivery, refund, and payout. The who is the authenticated actor, attached at the route boundary. Never contains a flag or a solver body.

Access control

  • Fail closed on a missing payment key. getMidtransClient throws in production when MIDTRANS_SERVER_KEY is unset rather than falling back to the offline client. That fallback plus /api/payments/offline would be a free checkout — a buyer marking their own order paid. The offline route independently refuses to run in production, because the failure mode is bad enough to deserve two locks.
  • Login is rate limited per source address and per account (src/lib/auth/rate-limit.ts). X-Forwarded-For is spoofable, which is why the per-account bucket exists. scrypt is expensive by design, so this bounds a CPU exhaustion vector as well as guessing.
  • Mutating /api/* requires same-origin when Origin is present (src/middleware.ts), on top of SameSite=strict session cookies. The Midtrans webhook is exempt: it is server-to-server and its authenticity comes from the signature, which is stronger.
  • Roles are re-read from the store on every guarded request, not trusted from the session token, so revoking a role takes effect immediately rather than at token expiry.

Content risk

Seller-authored text — a listing summary, a challenge.yml description, a review body — is rendered as JSX text, so React escapes it. There is no dangerouslySetInnerHTML anywhere in this repository, and adding one to render a writeup as markdown would introduce stored XSS in a buyer's authenticated session. If markdown rendering is ever wanted, it must have HTML disabled at the parser, not sanitized afterwards.

Sandbox output (Verification.log) is shown to sellers inside a <pre>. It is flag-scrubbed before storage and escaped on render.

See also: architecture, commerce, decisions/0004-sandbox-isolation.

On demand

Challenge bundle contract

≈1.2k · never verified · The on-disk format a seller uploads — directory layout, challenge.yml fields, and the three flag modes — read before touching parsing, building, or fulfillment

The format is a superset of CTFd's ctfcli challenge.yml, borrowing the release/server file split from CryptoHack's ctf-archive. Compatibility is a feature, not an accident: a purchased bundle should drop into a buyer's CTFd via ctf challenge push with no translation step.

Layout

<bundle>/
├── challenge.yml         # metadata, ctfcli-compatible superset
├── release_files/        # player-facing handout — chall.py, output.txt
├── server_files/         # secret; never delivered to players
│   └── generate.py       # reads $FLAG, writes release_files/   (mode: generate)
├── solver/
│   └── solve.py          # MUST print the flag to stdout
└── writeup.md            # author's solution; delivered to the BUYER, never public

solver/ and writeup.md are required to list. They are what make the challenge verifiable and what the buyer is actually paying for beyond the handout.

challenge.yml

ctfcli fields carried through unchanged: name, author, category, description, attribution, value, type, tags, topics, hints, files, connection_info, state, version.

Fields this marketplace adds, all under aya::

aya:
  scheme: rsa-weakness       # see [[crypto-taxonomy]]
  difficulty: medium         # easy | medium | hard | insane
  flag:
    mode: generate           # static | substitute | generate
    format: "ayactf{%s}"     # buyer-overridable at checkout
  solver:
    entrypoint: solver/solve.py
    profile: python-crypto   # python-crypto | sage
    timeoutMs: 60000
  license: event             # practice | event | unlimited

A literal flag in challenge.yml is rejected at parse time unless mode: static. This catches the most common authoring mistake before it reaches a sandbox.

The three flag modes

This is the part that is specific to selling crypto, and the reason the sandbox is on the fulfillment path.

ModeMechanismWhen
staticFlag is fixed; the bundle ships as uploaded.Legacy imports. The challenge cannot be re-flagged, so it is worth less and the UI says so.
substitute{{FLAG}} token is replaced in declared text files.Simple challenges where the flag appears verbatim.
generateserver_files/generate.py runs with $FLAG in env and rewrites release_files/.The real crypto case.
The generator's contract

The generator runs with the bundle mounted read-only at /work and an empty writable directory as its working directory (also exported as $OUT_DIR). So an author's ordinary open("output.txt", "w") lands in the right place without them knowing anything about the sandbox.

That working-directory choice is load-bearing: run the generator in /work instead and its first write fails with EROFS. RunSpec.workdir carries it, and verify.test.ts asserts the generate step asks for out while the solver step does not — a fake runner that writes wherever it likes will not catch a regression here on its own.

generate exists because a crypto flag is not present in the handout — it is encrypted into it. You cannot find-and-replace a flag inside an RSA ciphertext; you have to re-run the generator. That single fact is why fulfillment is a queued sandbox job rather than a file copy, and why generate mode is worth its complexity: without it, every sale of a challenge ships the same flag, and the first buyer's leak burns it for everyone.

Lifecycle of a bundle

  1. Inspect — extract safely (see the archive rules in security-guardrails), parse challenge.yml, check required paths, compute bundleHash.
  2. Build — mint an ephemeral flag, run the mode's mechanism in the sandbox, produce release files.
  3. Verify — run solver/solve.py in the sandbox against the built release files, assert stdout contains the ephemeral flag. Record duration.
  4. Publish — allowed only on a passed verification matching the current bundleHash.
  5. Fulfill — rebuild with the buyer's derived flag and their chosen format, package with writeup.md and a LICENSE.txt, hand to Commerce.

Steps 2, 3, and 5 are the same sandbox primitive with different inputs.

Rejection reasons a seller sees

Missing solver/ · missing writeup.md · literal flag with a non-static mode · declared files that do not exist · archive that fails the traversal/size checks · a generate mode whose generator does not write every declared release file · a solver whose stdout does not contain the flag.

See also: architecture, crypto-taxonomy, security-guardrails, decisions/0003-flag-modes.

Commerce — orders, Midtrans, escrow, licensing

≈1.0k · checked 2026-09-02 · The order state machine, Midtrans webhook handling, escrow and payout rules — read before touching anything that moves money

Commerce

Order state machine

States, and the only legal transitions. Anything not in this table is refused and audited.

FromToTrigger
createdawaiting_paymentMidtrans Snap token issued
createdexpired / cancelled / failedcheckout never got a token — TTL, buyer, or provider
awaiting_paymentpaidwebhook settlement / capture (accept)
awaiting_paymentexpiredwebhook expire, or TTL reached
awaiting_paymentfailedwebhook deny / cancel
awaiting_paymentcancelledbuyer cancels
paidfulfillingfulfillment job enqueued
fulfillingdeliveredartifact written, download token issued
fulfillingfulfill_failedsandbox error after retries exhausted
fulfill_failedfulfillingadmin or automatic retry
fulfill_failedrefundedgive up, return funds
paidrefundedrefund before fulfillment
deliveredrefundedrefund inside the dispute window

delivered is terminal once the dispute window closes. refunded, expired, failed, and cancelled are terminal.

Fulfillment can fail after payment has succeeded. That is not an edge case — it is the normal consequence of running a generator in a sandbox on the order path, and fulfill_failed exists so that money never sits in a state with no operator action attached to it.

Midtrans

Snap checkout: QRIS, GoPay, virtual account, bank transfer.

  • Signature is mandatory: sha512(order_id + status_code + gross_amount + MIDTRANS_SERVER_KEY). A request that fails it is dropped and audited, never processed.
  • The webhook is the only source of truth. The browser returning from the payment page triggers a poll, never a transition.
  • transaction_status mapping: settlement/capture (with fraud_status: accept) → paid; pending → stay; deny/cancel → failed; expire → expired.
  • capture with fraud_status: challenge stays pending and is surfaced to an admin.
  • Webhooks duplicate and arrive out of order. Handling is idempotent: re-applying a transition already applied is a no-op returning 200, not an error and not a double-fulfill.
  • The amount charged is the server-computed amount from order creation. A gross_amount in a webhook body is used for signature verification, never as an authority on price.
Money representation

Integer IDR minor units, everywhere, in a branded type. No floats. No bare number crossing a plane boundary.

Escrow and payouts

Funds sit in pending on the seller's balance from delivered until the 72h dispute window closes, then move to payable. Platform commission is deducted at that transition and recorded, so a payout line is always reconstructible.

Payout release is manual in v1: an admin marks a payable balance paid and records a reference. Automated disbursement means KYC onboarding and is not worth it before there is volume.

An order is stamped payoutMaturedAt before its balance moves, so a crash between the two cannot double-credit a seller. listDisputeWindowClosed filters on that stamp, which is what makes maturePayouts safe to run on a timer and safe to run twice.

Licensing
TypeGrants
practicePersonal, non-public use. No running it as an event.
eventOne named CTF event, unlimited players, for its duration.
unlimitedAny number of events by the purchasing organization.

The license text is snapshotted onto the order at purchase. Changing a listing's license terms later must never retroactively change what somebody already bought.

Every delivered bundle carries a LICENSE.txt naming the buyer, the order, and the grant.

What this does not do

No cart, no subscriptions, no automated disputes beyond a refund action, no multi-currency. IDR only in v1, because Midtrans settles in IDR and a display-only currency conversion invites a rounding bug in exchange for nothing.

See also: domain-model, security-guardrails, decisions/0005-webhook-driven-orders.

Cryptography scheme taxonomy

≈778 · never verified · The crypto challenge archetypes a listing is tagged with, and what each implies for buyers and verification — read when touching taxonomy, search facets, or listing metadata

A buyer cannot read a crypto challenge before buying it without spoiling it. The scheme tag is therefore the single most load-bearing piece of listing metadata: it is how somebody decides whether a challenge fits the slot they need to fill in their event, without seeing it.

The taxonomy is data (src/lib/catalog/taxonomy.ts), not an enum scattered through the code, so adding a scheme — or later, a whole category — is a data edit.

Schemes

Scheme idNameRecognizable byTypical mechanics
rsa-weaknessRSA weaknesssmall e, shared/close primes, partial key leakHåstad, Coppersmith, common modulus, Fermat, Wiener
symmetric-blockBlock cipher misuseECB repeats, CBC with an oracleECB cut-and-paste, CBC bit-flipping, padding oracle
stream-otpKeystream reusereused nonce or one-time padXOR crib-dragging, many-time-pad
signatureSignature flawrepeated or biased nonce in ECDSA/DSAnonce-reuse key recovery, biased-k lattice
classicalClassical ciphersubstitution, transpositionfrequency analysis, cipher identification
hashHash weaknesslength-extension, collisions, weak MAC constructionlength-extension, birthday, MAC forgery
prngPRNG predictionMersenne Twister output, LCG, weak seedingstate recovery, seed brute-force, lattice on LCG
latticeLattice / knapsackhidden number problem, truncated LCG, knapsackLLL, Babai, HNP
eccElliptic curveinvalid curve, smooth order, singular curveinvalid-curve attack, MOV, Smart's attack
protocolProtocol flawkey exchange, oracle in a handshakesmall-subgroup, downgrade, replay

Two schemes are worth a listing's tags where a challenge genuinely spans both — a lattice attack on an RSA partial-key leak is honestly rsa-weakness + lattice.

Difficulty

Seller-stated: easy | medium | hard | insane, corroborated over time by buyer ratings.

Solver runtime is not difficulty. A Coppersmith attack that takes four minutes of CPU can be an easy challenge if the attack is obvious; a five-line xor can be brutal if spotting it is the whole puzzle. The verification record stores duration because it is an operational fact about the sandbox budget, and the UI must not present it as a difficulty signal.

Sandbox profiles

ProfileContentsFor
python-cryptoPython 3.12 + pycryptodome, gmpy2, sympy, pwntoolsThe large majority of challenges
sageSageMathlattice, ecc, and heavier rsa-weakness work

A listing declares its profile in challenge.yml. sage is a much larger image with a slower cold start, so it is opt-in rather than the default.

What buyers see before purchase

Scheme tags, difficulty, verification badge with date, file manifest (names and sizes only), hint count, writeup length, and reviews. Never handout contents, never the writeup body, never the solver.

See also: bundle-contract, domain-model.

0001 — Record architecture decisions

≈370 · never verified · Why this project keeps decision records, and the format they use

Status: accepted Date: [YYYY-MM-DD]

Context

Decisions with long-lived consequences get made in issues, chat, and code review, and then the reasoning is lost. Six months later nobody remembers whether a constraint was a careful trade-off or an accident, so it gets "fixed" and the original problem returns.

This costs more when AI agents work in the repository: an agent reads the current code, sees something that looks suboptimal, and improves it — undoing a deliberate choice it had no way to know about.

Decision

Record every significant decision as a numbered file in .wondev/memory/decisions/.

Significant means: hard to reverse, or surprising to a newcomer, or previously argued about. Routine choices do not need a record.

Each record uses this structure: Context, Decision, Consequences. Status is one of proposed, accepted, or superseded with a link to the record that replaced it.

Records are immutable. When a decision changes, write a new record and mark the old one superseded rather than editing history.

Consequences

Agents and humans get the reasoning, not just the result, which makes "why is this like this?" answerable without archaeology.

The cost is a few minutes per decision, and the discipline to notice a decision is being made at all.

Superseded records stay in the repository. That is intentional: the trail of what was tried and rejected is as useful as the current answer.

0002 — Catalog / Forge / Commerce planes

≈441 · never verified · Why the marketplace splits into three planes and why sandboxed execution is its own plane rather than a utility

Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-02

Context

A challenge marketplace has three concerns that fail differently: describing and finding things, executing untrusted code, and moving money. Bundling them produces a codebase where a sandbox bug is reachable from a search endpoint.

Options

A — Conventional layering (controllers / services / repositories). Familiar, but it puts the sandbox on the same footing as a string formatter. Nothing in the structure signals that one service runs code written by strangers.

B — Three planes: Catalog, Forge, Commerce. Execution gets a named boundary with its own entry points, so "does this path reach the Forge?" is answerable by reading imports.

C — Separate services from day one. Real isolation, at the cost of deployment and transactional complexity before there is a single user.

Decision

B. The Forge is a plane because what makes it dangerous is not its size, it is its kind. Naming the boundary is what makes the rule in security-guardrails — "seller code executes only inside the Forge sandbox" — mechanically checkable rather than a convention people remember.

The Forge is also the natural seam for C later: it already has a queue and a request/response contract, so moving it to a separate worker is a deployment change, not a rewrite.

Consequences

  • src/lib/forge/ is the only place child_process or Docker is touched. A child_process import anywhere else is a review-blocking finding.
  • Build, verify, and fulfill share one primitive, so isolation is implemented once.
  • Cross-plane calls go through public entry modules, which costs some indirection in exchange for a dependency graph that can be audited.

0003 — Per-buyer flags, and why `generate` mode exists

≈610 · never verified · Why every sale re-flags the challenge, why crypto forces re-running the generator, and what that costs

Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-02

Context

A CTF challenge is worth something only while its flag is unknown. Sell the same bundle to fifty buyers and one leak destroys it for all fifty — including for the seller, who can no longer list it. A marketplace that ignores this sells an asset it is simultaneously destroying.

Prior art converges on assigning a flag when a handout is downloaded rather than baking it in: GPN CTF 2025's flag-sharing post-mortem, and ctfer.io's chall-manager, both do this per team. A marketplace is the same problem with "team" replaced by "order".

Options

A — One flag per challenge. Trivial. Destroys the asset on first leak.

B — Token substitution. Replace {{FLAG}} in release files at delivery. Cheap, and wrong for most crypto: the flag is not present in an RSA ciphertext as text, it is encrypted into it. Substitution silently produces a challenge whose output no longer corresponds to its flag.

C — Re-run the author's generator with the buyer's flag. Correct for crypto, at the cost of executing seller code on the order fulfillment path.

Decision

Support all three as declared flag modes, with generate (option C) as the intended default for crypto. static exists for legacy imports and is marked as lower value in the UI, because a challenge that cannot be re-flagged genuinely is worth less.

Consequences

  • The sandbox is on the money path. Fulfillment can fail after payment succeeds, so the order state machine has an explicit fulfill_failed state with an operator action attached (commerce). This is the main cost of the decision and it was accepted deliberately.
  • Fulfillment is a queued job with retry, never a synchronous request.
  • Every delivered bundle is unique, so a leaked flag identifies the order it came from.
  • Sellers must write a generator that is deterministic given $FLAG and writes every declared release file. Verification catches violations before publish rather than at a buyer's first download.

Rejected: DRM on the artifact

Obfuscating or otherwise locking a delivered .py file was considered and rejected. The buyer must be able to read and run the challenge — that is the product. Per-order flags give attribution, not prevention, and the documentation says so plainly rather than implying a protection that does not exist.

0004 — Docker sandbox with a stub that cannot pass

≈539 · never verified · Why seller code runs in a hardened container, and why the no-Docker fallback is forbidden from producing a passing verdict

Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-02

Context

The "Verified solvable" badge is the marketplace's entire answer to "how do I know this challenge is any good when I can't look at it?". Producing it means running a stranger's Python. Not producing it means competing with a generic digital-goods store on price alone.

Options

A — Manual admin review. No execution risk, no scale, and the badge is an opinion.

B — In-process execution with a timeout. Cheap and catastrophic: a solver is arbitrary code with the app's filesystem, network, and environment — including MIDTRANS_SERVER_KEY.

C — Hardened container per run. Real isolation. Requires Docker on the host.

D — A third-party sandbox service. Removes the ops burden, adds a vendor on the critical path of publishing and fulfillment.

Decision

C, with the full control set in security-guardrails: no network, read-only root, non-root user, all capabilities dropped, no-new-privileges, memory/CPU/PID caps, host-side wall-clock kill, byte-capped output, one writable mount.

A stubRunner exists so the app boots and develops without Docker — and it is structurally forbidden from returning passed. It returns unverified.

Consequences

  • npm run dev works with no Docker; nothing can be published in that mode, which is correct rather than inconvenient.
  • The argv builder for docker run has an exhaustive test asserting every isolation flag. That test is a security control; changing it is changing a firewall rule.
  • Archive extraction is treated as a separate boundary with its own traversal, symlink, and zip-bomb checks, because a malicious bundle attacks during inspection, before any sandbox is involved.
  • Sage support means a second, much larger image; it is opt-in per challenge.

Rejected: trusting --network=none alone

Network isolation prevents exfiltration but not local resource exhaustion. The memory, PID, and wall-clock caps are not redundant with it — they are the controls that keep one hostile submission from taking down the queue for everyone.

0005 — Webhook-driven order state, Midtrans, IDR minor units

≈603 · never verified · Why payment state comes only from signed webhooks, why every transition is idempotent, and why money is an integer

Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-02

Context

Buyers and sellers are Indonesian, so the payment rails that matter are QRIS, GoPay, virtual account, and bank transfer. Stripe has no Indonesian entity; Midtrans Snap covers all four.

Every one of those rails is asynchronous. A bank transfer settles minutes or hours after the buyer leaves the checkout page. There is no moment where the browser knows the truth.

Decision

Order state advances only on a Midtrans webhook whose signature verifies as sha512(order_id + status_code + gross_amount + MIDTRANS_SERVER_KEY). The browser returning from checkout triggers a poll of server state, never a transition.

All transitions are idempotent and validated against the table in commerce. Webhooks duplicate, retry, and arrive out of order; re-applying a transition already applied returns 200 and does nothing, and an illegal transition is refused and audited rather than applied.

Amounts are integer IDR minor units in a branded type, and the authoritative amount is the one the server computed at order creation. A gross_amount from a webhook body is input to signature verification and nothing else.

Consequences

  • A working local dev loop needs a way to simulate webhooks; a signed-payload test helper is part of the commerce plane, not an afterthought.
  • Order TTL and the expire webhook both have to be handled — the webhook can be missed.
  • Refunds are recorded as state transitions with an audit entry, even when the actual money movement is performed by hand in the Midtrans dashboard in v1.

Rejected: trusting the redirect, "just for the happy path"

Treating a ?status=success redirect as payment is the classic marketplace vulnerability: the buyer controls the URL. It is tempting because it makes local development easy. The signed- webhook test helper exists specifically to remove that temptation.

Rejected: floats, and multi-currency display

number for money invites a rounding error that only shows up in reconciliation. IDR has no subunit in practice but the branded integer type is kept anyway, so adding a currency later is a type change rather than an audit of every arithmetic site. Display-only currency conversion was rejected outright: it adds rounding and staleness bugs and buys nothing while settlement is IDR.

0006 — CTFd-compatible bundle format

≈461 · never verified · Why the bundle is a superset of ctfcli's challenge.yml instead of a bespoke format

Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-02

Context

Every marketplace has to define what is being sold. The tempting move is a bespoke format tuned exactly to the product.

Decision

The bundle is a superset of CTFd ctfcli's challenge.yml, with the release_files/ ÷ server_files/ split from CryptoHack's ctf-archive, and marketplace- specific fields namespaced under aya:.

Why

  • The buyer's next action is already defined. They bought a challenge to run an event. A ctfcli-shaped folder means ctf challenge push and they are done. A bespoke format means the buyer writes a converter, and the marketplace has quietly made its own product more expensive to use.
  • Sellers already have inventory in this shape. A challenge from a past event can be listed by adding a solver/ and a writeup, not by re-authoring it.
  • Namespacing under aya: keeps it valid. Unknown top-level keys are the usual way formats rot; a single namespaced key means a bundle stays loadable by tools that have never heard of this marketplace.

Consequences

  • Fields the marketplace does not use are carried through unchanged rather than dropped, so a round trip does not lose data.
  • CTFd's format is a moving target; the parser accepts unknown fields rather than rejecting them, and only validates what it relies on.
  • solver/ and writeup.md are marketplace-required additions and are the two things that make a challenge sellable rather than merely runnable.

Rejected: importing directly from a CTFd instance in v1

An "import from your CTFd" button is a good v2 feature. It needs credential handling and an API client for something that only helps sellers who already run CTFd, so it does not earn a place ahead of the marketplace working end to end.

Domain model

≈729 · never verified · The entities of the marketplace and how they relate — read before adding a table, a field, or anything touching challenges, listings, or orders

The distinction that carries the most weight: a Challenge is authored, a ChallengeVersion is immutable, and a Listing is commercial. Verification binds to a version, pricing binds to a listing, and delivery binds to an order. Collapsing any two of these breaks a rule in architecture.

Entities

EntityHoldsNotes
Useridentity, `roles: (buyer \seller \admin)[]`One account can buy and sell.
Challengeseller, title, slug, category, current versionThe authored thing, mutable metadata.
ChallengeVersionbundleHash, manifest, flag mode, storage keyImmutable. A new upload is a new version, never an edit.
Verificationversion, runner kind, verdict, duration, log refVerdict: `passed \failed \unverified \error`.
Listingversion, price (IDR), license type, stateState: `draft \pending \published \rejected \delisted`.
Orderbuyer, listing, amount, state, Midtrans ref, flag formatAmount is frozen at creation. See commerce.
Licenseorder, type, terms snapshotWhat the buyer may do, captured at purchase time.
Deliveryorder, artifact key, download count, expiryThe materialized per-buyer bundle.
Revieworder, rating, bodyPurchase-gated; one per order.
PayoutBalanceseller, pending / payable / paidMoves to payable after the dispute window.
AuditEntryactor, action, subject, timestampAppend-only.

Relationships

User(seller) 1─* Challenge 1─* ChallengeVersion 1─* Verification
                                      │
                                      1
                                      *
                                   Listing 1─* Order 1─1 License
                                                   │
                                                   1─1 Delivery
                                                   1─0..1 Review

Rules that live in code, not in the reader's head

  • A Listing may enter published only when its ChallengeVersion has a Verification with verdict passed whose bundleHash equals the version's current hash.
  • Uploading a new bundle creates a new ChallengeVersion. Existing Orders keep pointing at the version they bought — a buyer's purchase never changes under them.
  • A Review requires an Order in state delivered belonging to the reviewer.
  • PayoutBalance moves pending → payable only after the order's dispute window closes with no refund.
  • Prices are integer IDR minor units. Never a float. Never a currency-less number.

Deliberate omissions in v1

No carts (one listing per order), no bundles/collections, no subscriptions, no seller storefronts beyond a profile, no messaging between buyer and seller. Each is a seam, not a plan.

See also: architecture, bundle-contract, commerce.

Glossary

≈406 · never verified · Domain terms used in this codebase and what they precisely mean

Bundle — the on-disk artifact a seller uploads: challenge.yml, release files, server files, solver, writeup. See bundle-contract.

Bundle hash — content hash of a ChallengeVersion. Verification binds to it; if it changes, the verification is void.

Build — producing release files for a given flag, by the version's flag mode. Not "compiling" anything.

Verify — running the seller's solver against a freshly built challenge and asserting it recovers the flag. Produces the "Verified solvable" badge.

Fulfill — building for a buyer's flag and packaging the deliverable. Same sandbox primitive as build, different caller and different flag.

Forge — the plane that owns the sandbox. Never a build tool.

Flag mode — static, substitute, or generate. Determines how a bundle is re-flagged.

Derived flag — a buyer's flag, computed as KDF(secret, version + order). Never stored.

Ephemeral flag — a throwaway random flag used during verification only.

Scheme — a crypto challenge archetype (rsa-weakness, lattice, …). The primary way a buyer filters. See crypto-taxonomy.

Profile — a sandbox image: python-crypto or sage.

Release files — what the buyer's players receive. Server files — secret, never delivered to players.

Dispute window — 72h after delivered, during which a refund is possible and the seller's balance stays pending.

Listing vs Challenge vs ChallengeVersion — commercial wrapper vs authored thing vs immutable snapshot. See domain-model.

See also: architecture, domain-model.

Skills

changing-the-money-path

≈520 · Use when touching src/lib/commerce/ — orders, the state machine, Midtrans webhooks, escrow, refunds, licenses, or payouts.

A bug here does not throw an exception. It silently charges the wrong person, delivers something twice, or leaves funds in a state with no operator action attached.

Before you edit

Read the transition table in commerce. It is the specification. If your change needs a transition that is not in it, the table changes first — in the memory doc and the test — and the code follows.

The checklist

  • ☐ Is every new transition idempotent? Midtrans retries and duplicates. Applying the same webhook twice must be a no-op returning 200, not an error and not a double-fulfill.
  • ☐ Is the signature verified before anything else happens — sha512(order_id + status_code + gross_amount + SERVER_KEY)?
  • ☐ Does any code path advance state from a client request rather than a webhook? The redirect from checkout triggers a poll, never a transition.
  • ☐ Is the amount the server-computed one from order creation? A gross_amount off the request body verifies a signature and is authoritative for nothing.
  • ☐ Is money still an integer in minor units all the way through? No float, no bare number crossing a plane boundary.
  • ☐ Does an illegal transition get refused and audited, rather than ignored?
  • ☐ If fulfillment can now fail in a new way, does the order land in fulfill_failed with an operator action — never stranded in fulfilling?
  • ☐ Are license terms still snapshotted onto the order? Editing a listing must never change what somebody already bought.
  • ☐ Is there an audit entry with an actor for every state change?

Tests to run

npm test -- commerce
npm run typecheck

The state machine test is exhaustive: every legal transition asserted to work, and every illegal one asserted to be refused. Adding a state means adding a full row and column, not a happy-path case.

Use the signed-webhook test helper rather than loosening signature verification for local development. That helper exists precisely so nobody is tempted to add a bypass.

changing-the-sandbox

≈535 · Use when touching anything in src/lib/forge/ — the runner, the docker argv builder, archive extraction, build, verify, or fulfill. This code executes strangers' Python.

Everything under src/lib/forge/ runs code written by people who are not your users and not your colleagues. Treat a change here the way you would treat a change to a firewall rule.

Before you edit

  1. Read security-guardrails — the control table is the specification, not a suggestion.
  2. Identify which of the three callers you are affecting: build, verify, or fulfill. fulfill is on the money path; a regression there fails orders that have already been paid for.

The checklist

  • ☐ Does any new code path execute, import, or spawn bundle content outside a container? If yes, stop — that is the one rule with no exceptions.
  • ☐ Does the docker run argv still carry every isolation flag? Run the argv test.
  • ☐ Is the wall-clock timeout enforced host-side, with a docker kill — not by trusting the container to exit?
  • ☐ Is captured output still byte-capped before it is buffered, not after?
  • ☐ Can the flag for this run reach a log, an audit entry, a persisted capture, or an error message? Scrub it.
  • ☐ If you touched extraction: traversal, absolute paths, symlinks escaping the tree, uncompressed-size cap, and file-count cap — all still checked before the first write?
  • ☐ Can stubRunner now return passed through any path, including a default in a switch or an optional field? It must not.
  • ☐ Is the per-run directory still created under the dedicated root and deleted afterwards, including on the error and timeout paths?

Tests to run

npm test -- forge
npm run typecheck

The argv builder test is exhaustive on purpose. If your change makes it fail, the correct response is almost never to update the expectation — it is to ask which isolation property you just dropped.

When a control genuinely has to change

Write it down. Update the control table in .wondev/memory/security-guardrails.md in the same change, and add a decision record if you removed a control rather than added one. A guardrail that is weakened silently is how the next person concludes it was never important.

code-review

≈459 · Use when reviewing a diff, a pull request, or code just written — including your own, before declaring it finished

A review that lists everything it noticed is worse than one that names the two things that matter. Rank by consequence, and say plainly when there is nothing serious to report.

Steps

  1. Understand the intent. What was this change supposed to do? Review against that, not against the reviewer's preferred design.
  2. Read the diff completely before commenting. A confusing line often explains itself forty lines later.
  3. Look for defects first, in this order:
    • Wrong behaviour: off-by-one, inverted condition, wrong variable, missing await.
    • Unhandled cases: empty input, null, failure paths, concurrent access.
    • Security: unvalidated input reaching a query, a shell, a filesystem path, or a rendered page. Secrets in code or logs.
    • Resource handling: things opened and not closed, unbounded growth.
  4. Then look for durability: names that mislead, duplicated logic that will drift, an abstraction covering one case, missing tests for the new behaviour.
  5. Rank by consequence. What breaks in production, what breaks in six months, what is merely taste. Say which is which.
  6. Give each finding a failure scenario. "This is fragile" is not actionable. "With an empty items array this throws at line 42" is.

Rules

  • Distinguish a defect from a preference, explicitly. Both are worth saying; conflating them wastes the author's judgement.
  • Suggest the fix when it is short. Describe the problem when it is not.
  • Do not invent findings to seem thorough. "No blocking issues" is a legitimate result.
  • Check the tests as carefully as the code. Tests that assert nothing are a common defect.

Done when

  • Every finding names a file, a line, and what actually goes wrong.
  • Findings are ordered by severity, with taste-level notes marked as such.

debugging

≈457 · Use when investigating a bug, a failing test, or any behaviour that differs from what was expected — before proposing or applying a fix

The failure mode this skill prevents is guessing: changing something plausible, seeing the symptom disappear, and calling it fixed. That leaves the real defect in place and adds a change nobody can justify.

Steps

  1. Reproduce it. Find the smallest command or input that shows the failure every time. If it only fails sometimes, say so explicitly and treat frequency as data.
  2. Read the actual error. The full message, the full stack, the line it names. Do not skip to the fix because the error "looks familiar".
  3. State what you expected. Write the expected behaviour and the observed behaviour side by side. Vague expectations produce vague fixes.
  4. Locate it before changing it. Narrow to the specific line or condition, using whatever is cheapest: bisecting the input, logging intermediate values, or reading the code path top-down. Confirm the location before editing.
  5. Explain the mechanism. Say why this code produces this symptom. If that sentence cannot be written, the cause has not been found yet — go back to step 4.
  6. Fix the cause. Not the symptom. Suppressing an error, adding a null check at the crash site, or widening a type usually hides the defect rather than removing it.
  7. Prove it. Re-run the reproduction from step 1 and show the output. Add a test that fails without the fix and passes with it.

Rules

  • One hypothesis at a time. Changing several things at once destroys the evidence.
  • Revert failed attempts before trying the next idea, so the tree stays clean.
  • If a fix works but the mechanism is still unclear, say so rather than implying confidence.

Done when

  • The reproduction from step 1 now passes, and its output has been shown.
  • A test covers the defect.
  • The mechanism can be stated in one sentence.

git-workflow

≈420 · Use when committing, branching, or preparing a pull request — and before any command that rewrites history

Before committing

  1. Read the diff. git diff for unstaged, git diff --staged for staged. Never commit changes that have not been looked at.
  2. Check for accidents: debug prints, commented-out experiments, secrets, .env files, large binaries, unrelated formatting churn.
  3. Confirm the tests pass, and confirm it by running them.

Commits

  • One logical change per commit. A commit that both fixes a bug and renames a module is two commits.
  • Subject line in the imperative, under ~70 characters: add retry to token refresh, not added retries or fixes.
  • The body explains why, since the diff already shows what. Skip it when the subject is genuinely sufficient.
  • Never commit generated output that the build reproduces, unless the project deliberately vendors it.

Branches and pull requests

  • Branch from an up-to-date default branch. Do not commit directly to it.
  • Name branches after the change: fix-expired-token-refresh.
  • A pull request description says what changed, why, and how it was verified. Include the command output that proves it.

Rules

  • Destructive commands — reset --hard, push --force, checkout -- over local changes, clean -fd — require confirmation from the human first. Prefer push --force-with-lease when a force push is genuinely needed.
  • Never skip hooks (--no-verify) to get a commit through. A failing hook is information.
  • Do not amend or rebase commits that have already been pushed and shared.
  • Do not commit or push unless it was asked for.

Done when

  • The diff has been read, the tests have been run, and the message explains the reasoning.

planning-work

≈390 · Use before starting any task that spans more than one file or one obvious edit — plan before writing code

The purpose of a plan is to surface the wrong assumption before it becomes a day of work. Plans that only restate the request do not do that.

Steps

  1. Restate the goal in one sentence, in terms of the outcome rather than the mechanism. If it cannot be stated in one sentence, the task needs splitting before it needs planning.
  2. Find the constraints. Existing patterns to follow, interfaces that cannot change, data that must be migrated, things that must keep working. Read the code; do not guess.
  3. Name the uncertainty. What is genuinely unknown? Decide whether to resolve it now or proceed under a stated assumption. Write the assumption down.
  4. Break it into steps that can each be verified. A step whose completion cannot be checked is not a step, it is a hope. Order them so something works early.
  5. Identify what could go wrong and what the response would be. One line each.
  6. Confirm the scope. State what is deliberately not included, so it is a decision rather than an omission.

Rules

  • Plan against the code as it is, not as it is remembered.
  • Prefer the smallest change that fully solves the problem. Ambition belongs in the design discussion, not smuggled into an unrelated task.
  • If the task turns out to be several independent projects, say so and plan only the first.
  • Do not plan past the first real unknown. Resolve it, then continue.

Done when

  • Each step has a way to tell whether it worked.
  • Assumptions and excluded scope are written down, not implied.

verify-before-done

≈404 · Use before claiming that work is complete, fixed, passing, or ready to merge — evidence must come before the claim

"It should work now" is not a result. This skill exists because the gap between believing something works and having watched it work is where most wasted time lives.

Steps

  1. List the claims about to be made. "Tests pass", "the bug is fixed", "the build is clean" are three separate claims needing three separate proofs.
  2. Run the command for each claim. Not a similar command — the actual one. A passing unit test does not prove the build compiles.
  3. Read the output. Exit code and the last lines. A suite that ran zero tests exits zero.
  4. Quote the evidence when reporting. The command and its relevant output, not a paraphrase.
  5. Report what failed, plainly. Partial completion reported honestly is useful; partial completion reported as done destroys trust in every later report.

Claims and their proof

ClaimProof
tests passfull test command, showing the pass count
the bug is fixedthe original reproduction, now succeeding
it buildsthe build command, exit code zero
types are cleanthe typecheck command, no errors
it works end to endthe app actually run, not just its tests

Rules

  • Never claim a command succeeded without running it in this session.
  • Never describe expected output as if it were observed output.
  • If something was not verified, say which parts were not, rather than staying silent.
  • A skipped or filtered test run is not a passing test run. Say which was used.

Done when

  • Every claim has a command behind it, and every command has been run and read.

writing-tests

≈441 · Use when adding a feature or fixing a bug, before writing the implementation code

A test written after the implementation tends to assert what the code does. A test written first asserts what the code should do. Only the second kind catches a mistake.

Steps

  1. Write the failing test first. Name it after the behaviour, not the function: rejects an expired token, not test_validate.
  2. Run it and watch it fail. A test that has never failed proves nothing. Confirm it fails for the intended reason, not because of a typo or a missing import.
  3. Write the minimum code that passes. Resist building for requirements that have not been asked for yet.
  4. Run the full suite. A new test passing while an old one breaks is not progress.
  5. Refactor with the tests green. Now that behaviour is pinned, improve the shape of the code. Re-run after each change.

What to test

  • The behaviour a user or caller depends on.
  • Boundaries: empty, one, many, maximum, and one past the maximum.
  • The error paths. Untested error handling is usually broken error handling.

What not to test

  • Private helpers, directly. Test them through the public surface that uses them.
  • Language or framework behaviour. Assume the standard library works.
  • Exact log strings or incidental formatting, unless a consumer parses them.

Rules

  • Never weaken an assertion to make a test pass. If it fails, either the code or the expectation is wrong — decide which, and say so.
  • Never delete or skip a failing test to get a green run. A skipped test is a silent regression.
  • Tests must not depend on execution order or on each other's leftover state.

Done when

  • Every new behaviour has a test that fails without the change.
  • The full suite passes, and its output has been shown rather than assumed.

Subagents

code-reviewer

≈301 · Delegate when a change is large enough that reviewing it would crowd out the work — a wide diff, a refactor across many files, or anything touching code you have not read this session

You are reviewing a change you did not write. You have your own context window, so nothing from the conversation that dispatched you is visible — read what you need.

What to do

  1. Read the diff first, then read enough of the surrounding code to know whether the diff is right. A change can be locally correct and still wrong for the file it lands in.
  2. Look for the three things that actually break: a case the code does not handle, a behaviour change nobody asked for, and a claim in a comment or message that the code does not support.
  3. Check the tests. A test that would pass before the change is not a test of the change.

What to return

A list of findings, each with a file and line, and for each one a concrete way it fails: the input, the state, and what happens. If you cannot describe how it fails, you have found a preference, not a defect — leave it out.

Return the findings, not the file contents. The agent that dispatched you can read the files; what it cannot do is spend its context discovering what you already found.

If the change is sound, say so plainly and stop. A review that manufactures findings to look thorough costs more than it returns.

Commands

/new-scheme

≈183 · Add a cryptography scheme to the marketplace taxonomy

Add a new crypto scheme to the taxonomy.

Ask for the scheme id (kebab-case), display name, the tell that identifies it, and the typical mechanics, then:

  1. Add the entry to src/lib/catalog/taxonomy.ts, in the same shape as the existing ones.
  2. Add the row to the table in .wondev/memory/crypto-taxonomy.md, keeping the two in sync.
  3. Decide the sandbox profile it usually needs — python-crypto or sage — and say so if it is one of the heavier ones.
  4. Update the taxonomy integrity test: unique ids, every scheme reachable from the filter UI.
  5. Run npm test -- catalog and npx wondev build.

Do not add a scheme speculatively. A filter facet with no listings behind it makes the catalog look emptier than it is.

/onboard

≈149 · Explain this codebase to someone seeing it for the first time

Explain this repository to a competent engineer who has never opened it.

Cover, in this order:

  1. What the project does, in one paragraph.
  2. How to run it and how to test it — the actual commands, verified against the repository rather than assumed.
  3. The three or four directories that matter, and what belongs in each.
  4. The path a typical request or operation takes through the system, end to end.
  5. The two or three things that would surprise a newcomer, and why they are that way.

Prefer reading the code over reading the documentation, and say so when the two disagree.

/review

Review current changes

Review everything currently uncommitted in this repository.

  1. Read the full diff, staged and unstaged.
  2. Apply the code-review skill.
  3. Report findings ranked by consequence, each with a file, a line, and a concrete failure scenario — the input or state that makes it go wrong.
  4. If nothing serious is wrong, say so directly instead of padding the list with observations.

Do not change any code. This command reports; it does not fix.
